hints: Focus on what type of structure copper has, think giant metallic lattice rather than simple separate molecules.
Remember that in a metal the atoms lose their outer electrons to form positive ions surrounded by a sea of mobile electrons.
Consider which two particles attract each other strongly in that sea model, and why so much heat is needed to break that attraction to melt it.
walkthrough:
**Recall the structure of copper**

Copper is a metal, so picture a giant lattice, not single atoms sitting apart. Each copper atom contributes its outer electrons to a shared pool.

Model: $\text{Cu atoms} \rightarrow \text{Cu}^{n+} \text{ ions + delocalised } e^-$

**Identify the strong bonding force**

The strong force is the electrostatic attraction between the positive copper ions and the negative delocalised electrons all around them. This is metallic bonding.

Attraction: $\text{Cu}^{n+} \leftrightarrow \text{ delocalised } e^-$

**Link to high melting point**

Melting means making the particles move out of their fixed lattice positions. Because the ion to electron attraction is very strong, a lot of thermal energy is needed to loosen it, so the melting point is high.

options.A: Incorrect. Copper does not exist as neutral atoms only in its lattice. The outer electrons are delocalised, so describing attraction between atoms only misses the key metallic bonding particles.
options.B: Correct. Metallic bonding in copper is the strong electrostatic attraction between the lattice of positive copper ions and the sea of delocalised electrons. Breaking this strong attraction on melting requires a lot of energy, giving a high melting point.
options.C: Incorrect. Positive ions repel each other, they do not attract each other directly. The attraction that holds them together is mediated by the negatively charged delocalised electrons between them.
options.D: Incorrect. This mixes up the particles. In the metallic model the lattice particles are positive copper ions, not neutral copper atoms, attracted to the delocalised electrons.
